When nothing matches the list shows an empty table and 'Showing 0 of 0', with no message.
The filter's only button is the search icon; there is no clear control.
The success banner is shown once and cleared, with no timed hide.
An empty book shows 'You have no addresses yet.'
A search with no match shows 'No addresses match "<term>".' and a Clear search link.
A search with results shows a Clear search link.
The success banner hides itself after 3 seconds.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling and the prototype outrank the INS frontend: these are differences from Design Release 2.1 and none rests on persistence, validation, authentication or cross-service behaviour, so they go. The ruling's own open point on behaviour Design Release 2.1 does not show at all does not apply: the prototype shows its empty, search and banner states. Today's claims are not listed as overruled because the change requirements cite them as the evidence of what is removed.

conflicts.about: Where the address book is kept: the prototype holds it in one user's session; the real book is persisted by the address book service and shared by the organisation.

positions.says: Additions, edits and deletions are held in the user's prototype session only.
No address book API is called; entries live in the session.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as persistence, overrides it.
The book is scoped by organisation only, so every user of the organisation sees and changes the same book.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's persistence constraint wins: the book stays persisted in the address book service and organisation-wide. The prototype's session-only storage is set aside; what the user sees on each page is still the prototype's.

conflicts.about: Whether the address view page shows addresses found outside the book (a notification's consignment, contact or transporter addresses).

positions.says: The view page shows any address the service knows by id, looking in the book and then consignment, contact and transporter addresses.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as cross-service behaviour, overrides it.
The view page reads the address book service only, and anything it does not hold is not found.

conflicts.outcome: The cross-service constraint wins: a notification's addresses are copies held by the notification service, not the address book, so the INS view page reads the book only. How a notification shows its own addresses belongs to the journey areas.

conflicts.about: The row's View link: the prototype's bare 'View' against today's 'View <name>' with the name visually hidden.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides it.
Each row ends with a 'View' link.
Each 'View' link adds the address name in visually hidden text.

conflicts.outcome: Sighted users see the same 'View' either way. The hidden name meets the accessibility regulations the service must satisfy (distinct link purpose for screen reader users), a real constraint a visual prototype does not express, so it is kept. Nothing is overruled: the prototype's View link is built.

conflicts.about: The service navigation's items: the prototype shows Dashboard, Templates, Address book and Manage account; today's INS navigation also has Log out and no Templates.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as authentication, overrides it.
The navigation shows Dashboard, Templates, Address book and Manage account.
The navigation shows a Log out link to /auth/sign-out.

conflicts.outcome: Signing out is an authentication constraint the prototype cannot express, so Log out stays. The prototype wins on the rest: Address book is the active item on its pages here, and the Templates item is the shared layout area's change. Nothing is overruled.

conflicts.about: Whether an address-book record carries what the address can be used for (its uses), against the address book's ruling that it is untyped.

positions.says: The prototype wins by default over what the real services do today.
A saved address keeps every ticked use as its types, the first setting its primary type and address book type.
Ruling cv-044: the address book is untyped and unroled, so a supplied type gets a 400.
An address-book entry is untyped and owned by an organisation.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 wins: the record and its API gain the address's uses (req-1256). Storing them is something the prototype expresses, so no real constraint overrides it; it also meets cv-044's reason (one address used as consignor on one notification and consignee on the next) because an address carries several uses. cv-044's 'untyped and unroled' rule is set aside. repo-addressbook-p1-001 is not overruled: it is today's state, cited as the evidence for the new field. The rejection of stray 'type' and 'role' fields (repo-addressbook-p1-038, p2-016) can stay, since the new field carries its own name. DR1 inc-047 and inc-048 wait on exactly this typed record (document-dr1-parity-notes-p1-022, p1-023).

conflicts.about: Which countries the Country select offers: the prototype's fixed 42-country list with outermost regions, or the reference data list.

positions.says: A fix that is the content of a master reference-data list is deferred to MDM, not made in a hard-coded list.
inc-081: the real country list holds only sovereign states where DR1 offers regions and territories; blocked on MDM.
The Country select lists 'Select one' and 42 countries, including outermost regions and Crown dependencies.
Countries come from the reference data service's GET /countries.

conflicts.outcome: The DR1 judgement on the same difference (the country list's regions and territories, inc-081) wins: what the list holds stays with reference data and MDM (req-1235). The prototype still sets how the list is shown: alphabetical order (req-1231), United Kingdom pre-selected on add (req-1232), 'Select one' placeholder (req-1233), no placeholder on edit (req-1234).

conflicts.about: Where the address search's addresses come from: the prototype's made-up list shipped with the page, or a real address lookup.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as cross-service behaviour, overrides the prototype.
The search list is 500 made-up UK and EU addresses held in the prototype.
The lookup data also holds 80 generated Northern Ireland addresses.
Search runs in the browser over data that comes with the page; no lookup service is called.
The address lookup client calls the INS backend's GET /address-lookup with postcode= or find=, answered by a stub in stub mode.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's real-constraint clause wins: real users need real addresses, which only the address lookup service holds. The search keeps Design Release 2.1's look and type-ahead behaviour (req-647, req-1216) but its results come from the INS backend's /address-lookup (find=<term>), per environment: the lookup stub in the fit suites (the INS frontend's in-memory stub) and on the local stack, the INS backend's real lookup in CDP dev, and in CDP test, ext-test, perf-test and prod whatever c-217 settles. A picked result fills the fields by the spike's mapping (premises to line 1, street and locality to line 2, town, postcode); the lookup returns no organisation name, so the name is left for the user, and the country is United Kingdom because the search types are UK-only. Results show the lookup's formatted address line.

conflicts.about: Whether add and edit keep length limits and an email format check that Design Release 2.1 does not have.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as validation, overrides the prototype.
Only blank required fields are checked; no format rules and no length limits.
The edit form sets no format rule or message for email, phone or postcode, and no maximum lengths.
The record enforces maximum lengths and a valid email format.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's validation clause wins: today's length limits and email format check stay in the frontend and the API (req-1244), because the stored record has these limits and a malformed email cannot be used. Postcode and phone stay free text, as in both sources.

conflicts.about: Error-state accessibility the prototype leaves out: no 'Error:' title prefix, and error summary links to fields that stay hidden on the search layout.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as validation, overrides the prototype.
In the error state the page title has no 'Error:' prefix.
The add-address page title keeps no 'Error:' prefix when showing errors.
The edit page title keeps no 'Error:' prefix when showing errors.
On the search layout the fields the error summary links to stay hidden.
Errors prefix the title with 'Error: ', and each summary link moves focus to its field.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's validation clause wins: how validation errors reach users of assistive technology is part of validation the prototype does not express. Titles keep the 'Error: ' prefix (req-1246) and the search layout reveals its fields when it shows field errors (req-1285). Every error message and the page content otherwise follow Design Release 2.1.

conflicts.about: Prototype persistence behaviour: addresses held only in the session, edits that drop extra uses, and seeded addresses still shown with old details after an edit.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as persistence, overrides the prototype.
Saved addresses are kept only in the user's session.
Editing an address with several types saves it with only its first type.
A seeded address's edit is merged without replacing its stored lines, so the list can show the old address.
After a seeded address is edited, the list's Name column can still show the old name.
After the edit the list still showed the old name and address.
After saving, the list shows the edited values under the same address.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's persistence clause wins: addresses persist in the address-book service (req-1263), an edit keeps every use (req-1275) and the list shows what was saved (req-1276).

conflicts.about: Where templates live: the prototype's session with five seeded templates, or real persistence.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as persistence, overrides the prototype default.
Templates and deletions are held only in the user's session.
The service seeds five templates dated 15 April 2026.
Arena Aintree's card and answers.
Arena Aintree's answers in full.
Arena Aintree's movement details.
Shared values of every seeded template.
Rice Lane City Farm's card and answers.
Monk Park Farm's card and answers.
Acorn Farm's card and answers.
Glen Keen Farm's card and answers.
Seeded templates other than Arena Aintree have no contact or transport details.
Deleting a saved template that shares a seeded id brings the seeded one back.
A new template named like a deleted seeded one is saved but never listed.
The template page falls back to 'Date created: 15 April 2026' when a template has no date.
The templates journey makes no calls to other systems; templates are held in the session.
Five templates are seeded.
The seeded template cards' values.
The five seeded templates appear on the list.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first and names persistence as a real constraint the prototype cannot express: templates are stored by the backend and kept between sessions, and a user sees only templates really saved, with no seeded examples. The list order (newest saved first), the count, the card and every page design still stand; only the session storage and the seed data are set aside. Test suites may create their own templates through the journey.

conflicts.about: Who a stored template belongs to: the user who saved it, or their whole organisation.

positions.says: Templates have no owner, sharing or organisation scope.
No trace shows whether templates are shared across an organisation or private to their maker.

conflicts.outcome: A saved template is private to the signed-in user who saved it, stored against their user id and organisation, and listed under 'My templates'; nobody else sees, uses, changes or deletes it. The prototype wins by default and already keeps saved templates to the user who made them (held in their own session, never shared between users, under a 'My templates' heading); real persistence and sign-in only replace the session with a store keyed to that user, so nothing is left for a person to decide.

conflicts.about: What the templates list's 'Sort by:' select does, given the prototype never reorders and templates hold no arrival date.

positions.says: The sort value only preselects an option; the select is outside any form with no apply button, so sorting is not built.
The list has a 'Sort by:' select with Select one, Newest first, Oldest first and Arrival date.
No trace drives the select, so whether it reorders and how Arrival date applies is not shown.

conflicts.outcome: Build Manage templates' 'Sort by:' select as Design Release 2.1 has it: named sort, options 'Select one' (empty value), 'Newest first', 'Oldest first' and 'Arrival date', preselecting the option that matches the sort value in the address, outside any form and with no apply button. As in the prototype, the select does not reorder the list, so 'Arrival date' needs no meaning for templates; making the sort work would depart from the prototype with neither a DR1 judgement on this list nor a real constraint to justify it.

conflicts.about: Whether a template saves each consignment party's address, or only the place of origin copied into every party.

positions.says: A template saves only the place of origin and a contact address, records that the same address is used for every party, and using it copies the place of origin into consignor, consignee, importer and place of destination.
The template page lists Place of origin, Consignor, Consignee, Importer and Place of destination, each as a full address.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, including cross-service behaviour, overrides the prototype default.

conflicts.outcome: A template saves the place of origin, consignor, consignee, importer, place of destination and contact address each as answered, shows them on the template page's Addresses card (Place of origin, Consignor, Consignee, Importer, Place of destination) and Contact address card as the design renders them, shows the consignee and consignor names on the template card, and seeds each back into a notification started from it; the contact address falls back to the place of origin where none was chosen, as the design does. The design's single copied address is set aside because the real notification persists and sends each party separately, a cross-service constraint the prototype cannot express.

conflicts.about: Whether using a template seeds the transporter's country it saves and shows.

positions.says: Using a template seeds the transporter's name, address, approval number and type, but not the country.
A template saves the transporter's country.
The template page's Transport details card shows the transporter's Country.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as persistence, overrides the prototype default.

conflicts.outcome: Using a template seeds the transporter's country along with its name, address, approval number and type. The prototype's design saves and shows the country and, after a template is used, shows the same country again (worked out from the seeded approval number); the real service stores the country as an answer and has no approval number for a private transporter, so it carries the saved country into the new notification to give the same result.

conflicts.about: Saving a template by visiting /templates/save with a GET.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default.
A GET to /templates/save saves the template in progress, the same as Save template.
Visiting /templates/save during template creation saves the template.
GET /templates/save redirects and the suite reaches it.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first: a GET that saves bypasses the real services' request forgery protection, a constraint the prototype cannot express. A template is saved only by the 'Save template' form post from the review page, which still produces the same banner and list.

conflicts.about: Whether amend, cancel amendment and copy as new are started by links (GET) as the prototype draws them, or by form posts.

positions.says: The amend and cancel-amendment dialogs' confirm buttons and Copy as new are links to GET routes that change state.
State-changing actions are form posts carrying the CSRF crumb (and the concurrency token).
A real constraint the prototype cannot express (validation, authentication) overrides it.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first: a state change is a POST with the CSRF crumb, an authentication constraint the prototype cannot express. Each control looks and reads as Design Release 2.1 draws it (a button, a link-styled button) but submits a form. The prototype's claim is kept for where each control leads.

conflicts.about: Amend and cancel-amendment confirmations: a custom modal dialog (Design Release 2.1) or a separate confirmation page (today's cancel-amend).

positions.says: Both confirmations are modal dialogs opened over the review or view page.
The dialog is a custom component; GOV.UK Frontend has no modal, and a confirmation page would keep to the toolbox.
Cancel amendment is a separate GET/POST page at /notifications/{id}/cancel-amend.
The prototype wins by default over what the real services do today.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype wins: build the dialogs as drawn. No DR1 judgement covers them, and keeping to GOV.UK components is house practice, not one of the ruling's overrides. Because the action must work as a form post (c-189), each trigger also works without script: it reaches a confirmation page at today's route with the dialog's heading and buttons. Today's page claim is kept as the evidence for that route.

conflicts.about: Where confirming an amendment lands: the review page (Design Release 2.1) or the overview hub (today).

positions.says: After choosing to amend, the trader goes to the notification's review page.
Amend posts and lands on the notification's hub.
Amend redirects to the notification's task list hub.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype outranks the tests repo and today's traces: amending lands on the amend review. The tests and trace claims stay as the evidence of today's behaviour.

conflicts.about: Whether edits during an amendment are saved to the record, or held only in the session as the prototype does.

positions.says: Nothing is saved automatically while amending, and cancelling leaves edits in the session without writing them back.
Save keeps a notification in AMEND and persists it, with the submitted version held as a snapshot.
A persistence constraint the prototype cannot express overrides it.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first: the real service keeps saving amendment edits to the AMEND record behind the submitted snapshot. What the trader sees is the same as Design Release 2.1. The prototype claim is not overruled because it also backs draft autosave (req for drafts).

conflicts.about: Whether delete removes the notification (prototype) or soft-deletes it (today).

positions.says: Confirming the delete removes the notification.
Soft delete keeps the record and its content and sets the status to DELETED, publishing an event.
Persistence and cross-service constraints the prototype cannot express override it.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first: delete stays a soft delete with its events. To the trader it looks the same as the prototype's removal.

conflicts.about: Dashboard card actions: Copy as new and View only (Design Release 2.1's list) or the status-driven set (today).

positions.says: inc-030 rejected: keep the card's status-driven links; do not flatten to Copy as new and View.
A live-animals dashboard row offers Copy as new and View.
Cards show Resume, View, Amend, Copy as new, Cancel amendment and Delete by status.

conflicts.outcome: The DR1 judgement on this same difference outranks the prototype: the cards keep their status-driven actions. The prototype claim is not overruled because it also shows a deleted notification gone from the list.

conflicts.about: Whether DR1's inc-026 (treat the delete and cancel-amend pages as unassessed, raise nothing about their copy) stops the Design Release 2.1 copy changes.

positions.says: Delete and amend may be capabilities DR1 did not draw, so the pages need reviewing against DR2 designs, not DR1.
Until the designer settles scope, raise nothing about the pages' copy, buttons or wording.
The delete page is headed 'Delete this notification?' with Design Release 2.1's summary, wording and buttons.

conflicts.outcome: DR1 ranks above the prototype, and its judgement confines itself to the DR1 comparison and sends these pages to a DR2 comparison. Design Release 2.1 is that comparison, so its copy is adopted. Nothing is overruled.

conflicts.about: What a copy carries over: Design Release 2.1's list, the backend copy mapper's list, or everything but documents (what today's pages show).

positions.says: Copy carries import details, what is imported, reasons, additional details, parties and CPH, and clears counts, identifiers, arrival, transit, transporter, documents and contact address.
Copy keeps identification, commodity type and addresses, and resets logistics and per-animal counts, also clearing the internal reference, species, unweaned answer and exit date.
Today a copy's overview shows every task Complete except Upload documents.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype outranks both: a copy carries exactly Design Release 2.1's list, in the record and on the pages alike. Each field that differs is its own requirement. The backend and trace claims stay as evidence of today's behaviour.

conflicts.about: Copying a notification mid-amendment: the submitted version (prototype) or the edits in progress (today).

positions.says: Copy by reference uses the notification's saved snapshot, which an unfinished amendment does not change.
Copying an AMEND notification copies its current, edited content.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype outranks the backend: copy the submitted version. The backend already holds it as the amend snapshot, so no constraint stands in the way.

conflicts.about: Which dashboard the guards, delete and the view page's Back link return to: the overall dashboard (Design Release 2.1) or the live-animals dashboard and hub (today).

positions.says: After a delete the trader lands on the overall dashboard (titled Dashboard, h1 Import notification service); the guards and the view page's Back link go there too.
The dashboard is temporary in the animals frontend and moves to trade-imports-ins-frontend.
Delete returns to the live-animals dashboard at /live-animals?deleted=1.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype outranks today's frontend: these routes return to the overall dashboard, which in the real services is the INS front door's dashboard, where DR1's notes say the dashboard belongs. The live-animals list shows the deletion message on its next visit.

conflicts.about: What the trader sees when Continue on the amend review is refused because an answer is invalid: nothing (the amend trace) or the error summary the draft review shows.

positions.says: Continue on the amend review is silently held: the same page comes back with no error summary or message.
A draft's review lists incomplete sections in a GOV.UK error summary, each linking to its card.
An amendment can only be resubmitted once every task row is fulfilled.
The prototype (Design Release 2.1) wins by default over what the real services do today.

conflicts.outcome: Continue on the amend review is held while any answer is invalid or incomplete (such as an arrival date outside 7 days back to 6 months ahead): the trader stays on the amend review, and, as Design Release 2.1 draws and specifies it, no error summary or error message is shown. The draft review's error summary with a Complete <card> link per incomplete section is not carried over to the amend review: the prototype wins by default, DR1 judged nothing about the amend review, and the only real constraint (an amendment is resubmitted only once complete and valid) is met by the hold itself.

conflicts.about: Whether the reason for import is asked before or after commodity details in the opening run

positions.says: The step order starts origin, what are you importing, reason for import, consignment details.
The opening run visits origin, commodity search, consignment details, then import reason.
The documented opening run order puts consignment details before reason for import.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks the real frontend and no DR1 judgement or real constraint covers the order: the reason for import moves before commodity details. The frontend's run order (and its documentation) is set aside.

conflicts.about: Whether the CPH number page is a step of the journey after roles and addresses

positions.says: The step order has no CPH step; CPH is reached from within roles and addresses, which is followed by the contact address.
In the run, the addresses page and the CPH number page each stop the run when the notification needs them.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks the real frontend and nothing overrides it: 'Save and continue' on roles and addresses goes to the contact address, and the CPH number is reached only from its row on roles and addresses.

conflicts.about: Whether a page opened from the overview chains on through its section or returns to the overview

positions.says: A section page reached from the hub returns to the hub when it continues.
One task link carries the user through several pages before returning: reason on to additional details, roles and addresses on to CPH, arrival on to transit and transporter.
Once the task list has been shown, saving moves through its own section and returns to the task list at the section's end.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks the real frontend and no DR1 judgement or real constraint covers section chaining: a page opened from the overview returns to the overview on save. Every chained-to page has its own overview row, so nothing becomes unreachable.

conflicts.about: Where the opening run ends when the notification is still incomplete

positions.says: Review notification is always a step after the contact address, and the next page after a step is the following step.
The opening run reaches the review page only when every task row is ready; an incomplete run goes to the overview.
A run that reaches the review step while the notification is incomplete falls through to the task list.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks the real frontend: the run always ends on the review page, which already names what is outstanding. The frontend's divert-to-overview rule is set aside; its rule that a run with no open later step ends on the overview (repo-frontend-p1-113) still holds and is not overruled.

conflicts.about: Where a journey page's Back link goes

positions.says: Back goes to the template review when reached from one, to the overview when reached from the hub, and otherwise to the previous journey page.
In change mode Back still goes to the overview.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks today's behaviour: Back follows the page's context and otherwise the previous journey page. trace-animals-fit-p1-083 is not overruled because it also records that change-mode pages keep their return controls, which stays true.

conflicts.about: Whether the origin of the import page offers 'Save and return to overview' and 'Cancel and return to overview'

positions.says: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.
Rule (b): only the pages the overview links to end with the three return controls, built as ruled and not re-derived from the design.
inc-013 is rejected: the design's page-by-page button list, which showed origin with one button, is not ported.
The origin of the import page has no 'Save and return to overview' button.
The origin of the import page has no cancel link.

conflicts.outcome: DR1 already judged this difference (inc-161 rule (b), inc-013 rejected, which named the origin page among those the design gave one button), and the ruling makes a DR1 judgement on the same difference outrank the prototype: the origin page keeps all three controls.

conflicts.about: Whether the party pickers, CPH number page and permanent address page offer return-to-hub controls

positions.says: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.
Under rule (b) the CPH number page ends with the primary button alone.
Under rule (b) the party pickers end with the primary button alone.
The address selection, permanent address and CPH number pages offer 'Save and return to hub' and 'Cancel and return to hub'.

conflicts.outcome: DR1 rule (b) judged exactly this difference for the CPH number page and the party pickers, and the permanent address page is likewise reached from another page: they end with the primary button alone. trace-prototype-dr2-1-p13-027 is not overruled because it also backs the contact address page's wording (c-209), which is overview-linked and keeps its controls.

conflicts.about: Whether the contact address page's return controls say 'hub' or 'overview'

positions.says: The prototype wins by default over what the real services do today.
The contact address page words its controls 'Save and return to hub' and 'Cancel and return to hub'.
The task-list page is called 'Overview' on screen and 'hub' never appears to users.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks the frontend's own copy rule, and that rule is not a DR1 judgement departing from the prototype (DR1's inc-006 renamed hub to overview because DR1's design said overview). The contact address page reads 'Save and return to hub' and 'Cancel and return to hub'.

conflicts.about: Which controls the party pickers, the CPH number page and the permanent address page show while a notification is being amended

positions.says: While amending, every journey page shows 'Save and return' (to review), 'Save and continue' and a link-styled 'Save and return to overview'.
A page reached from another page, such as the CPH number page, ends with the primary button alone.

conflicts.outcome: While a notification is being amended, overview-linked pages get Design Release 2.1's full amend ending; the party pickers, the CPH number page and the permanent address page show 'Save and return' (primary, to the review page) and 'Save and continue' (secondary) only, without the link-styled 'Save and return to overview'. DR1 rule (b) is a judgement on where return-to-overview controls go, and the prototype itself answers that both ways in amend (the contact address page drops the hub button, the CPH page keeps it), the same split DR1 already ruled on, so rule (b) keeps the hub control off these pages; the review and continue buttons exist only in amend, DR1 never judged them, so the prototype default adds them. Outside amend these pages keep rule (b)'s primary button alone. Each position holds in part, so no claim is set aside whole.

conflicts.about: Whether 'Save and return to overview' skips a page's checks

positions.says: 'Save and return to overview' keeps the selection without validating.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as validation or persistence, overrides the prototype.

conflicts.outcome: On origin, what are you importing, main reason for import, identification, additional details, arrival details, transit countries, transporter, upload documents and roles and addresses, 'Save and return to overview' saves every answer given and returns to the overview even when a required answer is missing, as Design Release 2.1 does (the backend accepts any field missing or empty). An answer that fails its own format rule, such as an impossible date or a malformed region code, is refused with its error, because the real service cannot store a value that does not fit its field: a real persistence and validation constraint the prototype cannot express, which the ruling says overrides it. Consignment details, the CPH number page and the contact address page check their answers before saving, as Design Release 2.1 does.

conflicts.about: Whether the service navigation keeps a Log out item: Design Release 2.1 drops it, and the real services have it.

positions.says: In DR2.1 the service navigation has no Log out item, unlike design release 2.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as authentication, overrides the prototype default.
DR1 judged that sign-out sits in the service navigation as 'Log out', replacing the separate 'Sign out' link.
The Log out navigation item links to /auth/sign-out.

conflicts.outcome: Log out stays as the last navigation item on both frontends (req-969). The prototype has no real session to end, so leaving it out does not show a decision about sign-out. In the real services, Log out is the only way to end a Defra ID session, and the ruling lets an authentication constraint override the prototype. The rest of the prototype's list (Dashboard, Templates, Address book, Manage account) is adopted, so prototype-dr2-1-source-p1-021 and p1-018 still back the Templates requirement. Only the claim that drops Log out is set aside.

conflicts.about: Where the Address book navigation item goes: inside the same service in Design Release 2.1, or the INS frontend's address book in the real services.

positions.says: Under DR2.1 the address book sits under the service's own base path, at /design-release-2.1/address-book.
Rhys ruled that the dashboard and the address book are temporary in the animals frontend and move to trade-imports-ins-frontend.
Cross-service behaviour the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default.

conflicts.outcome: The Address book item goes to the INS frontend's /address-book from both frontends (req-1677). The address book is a shared capability in a separate service, which the single-service prototype cannot express. The prototype claim that places it under the service's own base is set aside. The item, its label and its place in the order still stand.

conflicts.about: Where the GOV.UK header logo and the service name link: Design Release 2.1 sends both to its index of design releases, which has no counterpart in a real service.

positions.says: The GOV.UK logo links to the service index (/design-release-2.1/index), and the service name in the service navigation does too.
On DR2.1 pages the header logo and the service name both link to the prototype index.
The GOV.UK header logo links to https://www.gov.uk/.
The service name links to the set's dashboard at /live-animals.
The GOV.UK header logo links to https://www.gov.uk/.
A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.

conflicts.outcome: Keep the current targets. The GOV.UK logo links to https://www.gov.uk/ on both frontends, as the GOV.UK header pattern does. The service name links to each frontend's dashboard home: /live-animals on the animals frontend and / on the INS frontend, wherever the dashboard area finally puts the dashboard. The prototype sends both links to its index of design releases, which is prototype tooling that is not built (req-1681), so it names no real destination to move them to; the prototype keeps a separate Dashboard item, so its index is not a stand-in for the dashboard. With no DR1 judgement on the header links, the real frontends' targets are the only buildable ones and stand.

conflicts.about: Where the phase banner's feedback link goes: a placeholder '#' in Design Release 2.1, or the APHA service desk mailbox in the real services.

positions.says: DR2.1 dashboard pages show an Alpha phase banner whose feedback link is a placeholder '#'.
Because the design's feedback link is a placeholder, DR1 ruled it to be mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk, and forbade inventing a /feedback route or survey URL.
The phase banner's feedback link is an email link to the APHA service desk.

conflicts.outcome: The feedback link stays mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk on both frontends (req-1684). DR1 already judged this same difference, a placeholder feedback link in the design, and a DR1 judgement on the same difference outranks the prototype. The INS frontend already uses the same destination. The Alpha banner itself is shown by today's claims, so setting aside the prototype's placeholder claim loses nothing.

conflicts.about: Whether service pages show the signed-in user's email and 'Home' and 'About' links, as the tests repo's shared page object suggests.

positions.says: The signed-in user's email or name is shown nowhere, and there is no 'Sign out' link outside the navigation's Log out.
Every service page offers Home, About, Log out, Address book and Dashboard links and shows the signed-in user's email (inferred from the shared base page object).

conflicts.outcome: No page shows the signed-in identity (req-1702). The frontend outranks the tests repo, the end-to-end traces show no identity (trace-e2e-p1-040), and the tests repo's own dashboard spec asserts no email (repo-tests-p4-057). The base page object's Home, About and email locators are stale helpers that no spec asserts. They can be removed whenever the tests repo is next touched.

conflicts.about: Which environments the address searches run in: the INS backend's address lookup is set up only on the local stack (a stub) and in CDP dev, while Design Release 2.1 searches everywhere.

positions.says: The add-address pages for consignee, importer and place of destination start with a UK address search that offers matching addresses as you type.
The address book's add-details step searches United Kingdom addresses from the lookup list.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as cross-service behaviour, overrides the prototype.
The address lookup is used only by the spike page, which is registered in dev and local environments, never in test, perf or production.
In test, perf-test, ext-test, prod and the other environments the spike does not exist.
In stub mode, outside production, lookups are answered by an in-memory stub instead of the INS backend.
The lookup is a spike, not a live feature, and how the real build would use one is still to be decided.

conflicts.outcome: Neither precedence nor the ruling settles it: the ruling's real-constraint clause (c-178) says the search must use the real lookup, but that lookup is set up only in CDP dev, so Design Release 2.1's search cannot be met as written in CDP test, ext-test, perf-test or prod. The default gives each environment what it can run.
conflicts.question: Should the INS backend's address lookup be set up in CDP test, ext-test, perf-test and prod so the address searches work there, or should those environments offer manual address entry only?
conflicts.default: Each environment gets: in the fit suites (stub mode) and on the local compose stack, the searches run against the lookup stub's fixed results; in CDP dev, against the INS backend's real lookup; in CDP test, ext-test, perf-test and prod, the searches are built behind a per-environment setting left off, so every searching add-address page and the commercial transporter form open with the address and contact fields shown and no search box (as the 'Origin or Consignor' step does, req-1213) until the lookup is set up in that environment. Every field, message and save is the same in every environment.

conflicts.about: How the commercial transporter's Northern Ireland-only address search is built when the lookup stubs return only London addresses.

positions.says: The commercial transporter page's address search searches the Northern Ireland lookup addresses.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as cross-service behaviour, overrides the prototype.
The lookup stub returns the same three addresses as the stack's address lookup simulator whatever postcode or term is searched.
The stub serves the same three SW1A 1AA addresses for every search.
Today every commercial transporter address field is typed by hand; there is no address search.

conflicts.outcome: Neither precedence nor the ruling settles it: Design Release 2.1's Northern Ireland-only search comes from a made-up list (overruled by c-178), and the real lookup's stubs hold no Northern Ireland address, so a Northern Ireland search cannot be seen in the fit suites or on the local stack as things stand. The default says what each environment gets.
conflicts.question: Should the commercial transporter's search use the same INS backend address lookup limited to Northern Ireland (BT) postcodes, with the lookup stubs given Northern Ireland addresses so the search can be seen outside CDP dev?
conflicts.default: The commercial transporter search calls the same INS backend lookup (find=<term>) and lists only results whose postcode starts 'BT'. The lookup stubs used by the fit suites and the local stack gain a few Northern Ireland addresses with BT postcodes, returned for a search, so the filter and the fill (req-457) can be seen there; CDP dev gets the real lookup's Northern Ireland results; CDP test, ext-test, perf-test and prod get what c-217 gives them.
